text: Imagine waking up alone on Mars, after a crash, with less than two hours of oxygen in your suit. Where would you find air, water, and shelter? We are Team Butterfly from Kumila Bangladesh. Shagoto Chodhuri, Tamima Rahman Chuiti, Moitrib Homik Buja, Mahamadraihanul Hasan, Sifula Ibneriza, and Uma Iman Monea. Six people, one goal. To make the real Mars something anyone can explore, not just read about. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we built Martian Story, a walkable, survivable map of Jezero Crater, the place where NASA's Perseverance Rover landed, made entirely from NASA's open data. Our challenge is the Interplanetary Survival Guide, Martian Map. Future crews will need to know a place on Mars before they land, where the ground is safe to walk, what the rocks are made of, how cold the nights get, and what it takes to make air and water. That knowledge already exists. NASA has mapped Jezero in astonishing detail, and Perseverance has driven more than 45 kilometers across it. But it is scattered across scientific archives, in formats only specialists can open. Here is how precise it is. At the Perseverance landing site, our terrain reads minus 2,569.92 meters. NASA's recorded value is 0.91, one centimeter apart. We wanted anyone, a student, a teacher, a future astronaut, to stand on that ground and understand it. Martian Story puts that place in a web browser. The terrain is the USGS Mars 2020 High-Rise Digital Terrain Model, one meter per pixel, shaded by the High-Rise Ortho-Mosaic. The crater rim comes from the CTX Elevation Model, and the MOLA Laser Altimeter. Press K and minerals measured by the MRO-CRISM Spectrometer light up the ground. Olavine, Carbonate, and Hydrated Minerals that could give up water. The blue line is Perseverance's real traverse, from NASA's MMGIS maps. Press P and you see the Mastcam Z and Navcam photos the rover took right here, its rim-fax radar showing the layers underground, and the weather from Meda, its own weather station, right now minus 60 degrees at 700 pascals. And there is Perseverance itself, NASA's own 3D model parked on its real waypoint. Eleven NASA data sets working together in one place. Every survival rule follows the science. Oxygen comes from a Moxie-style electrolyzer. Water is baked out of sulphate minerals. Power follows the real Martian Sun from NASA's Mars 24 clock, and radiation is counted against Curiosity's dose measurements. Fourteen missions take you from your first breath to a launch home. Students learn Mars by walking on it. Teachers get a free classroom tool that needs no install, and anyone can see NASA's data together in one place. Next, we want more landing sites, a guided classroom mode, and multiplayer crews who plan a base together. Martian's story was built by Team Butterfly, with open data from NASA, USGS, and JPL. Code was written with help from AI assistants, and this narration was generated with 11 labs. Full credits are on our project page. Thank you.
